[`cppODE()`](../reference/cppODE.html), [`cvode()`](../reference/cvode.html)
and [`cppFUN()`](../reference/cppFUN.html) share one code generator for
equations in the syntax of [`expressions`](../reference/expressions.html).
Symbols follow the [notation table](methods-overview.html#notation).

## Expression graph and emitted code {#codegen}

The generator emits straight-line C++ templated over the scalar type, one
source for value, dual and nested-dual instantiations. Automatic
differentiation [@griewank2008evaluating] on an expression graph forms
the Jacobian, the discrete-adjoint contractions, and the time derivatives
of right-hand side and event roots at code-generation time.

**Expression graph.** Python's parser reads each expression into a
directed acyclic graph. States, parameters, forcings, time and constants
are leaves; sums, products, powers and function calls are inner nodes.
Nodes are hash-consed [@ershov1958programming; @filliatre2006hashconsing]:
identified by operation, operands and constant attributes, each is
created once, so a repeated subexpression is one node without an
elimination pass. Sums and products are flat with numeric coefficients
and exponents; equal constants are one node. SymPy reads syntax the
parser does not and differentiates functions without a graph rule.

```{r expression-graph, fig.width = 4.6, fig.height = 3.6, dpi = 96, fig.align = "center", out.width = "60%", fig.cap = "Expression graph of $f_A = f_B = -k_1 A B + k_2 C$ and $f_C = k_1 A B - k_2 C$; edge labels are coefficients."}
# leaves at the bottom, operations as circles, roots at the top
pos <- list(k1 = c(0, 0), A = c(1, 0), B = c(2, 0), C = c(3, 0), k2 = c(4, 0),
            u = c(1, 1.3), v = c(3.5, 1.3), s = c(1.5, 2.6), r = c(3, 2.6),
            fs = c(1.5, 3.6), fr = c(3, 3.6))
radius <- c(k1 = 0.2, A = 0.2, B = 0.2, C = 0.2, k2 = 0.2, u = 0.27, v = 0.27,
            s = 0.27, r = 0.27, fs = 0.25, fr = 0.25)
edge <- function(from, to, label = NULL, side = 2) {
  p <- pos[[from]]; q <- pos[[to]]
  d <- (q - p) / sqrt(sum((q - p)^2))
  a <- p + radius[[from]] * d; b <- q - radius[[to]] * d
  arrows(a[1], a[2], b[1], b[2], length = 0.08, angle = 20)
  if (!is.null(label)) {
    m <- (a + b) / 2
    text(m[1], m[2], label, pos = side, cex = 0.8, offset = 0.3)
  }
}
op <- par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
plot.new()
plot.window(xlim = c(-0.4, 4.4), ylim = c(-0.3, 3.9), asp = 1)
for (n in c("u", "v", "s", "r"))
  symbols(pos[[n]][1], pos[[n]][2], circles = radius[[n]], inches = FALSE, add = TRUE)
text(pos$u[1], pos$u[2], "\u00d7"); text(pos$v[1], pos$v[2], "\u00d7")
text(pos$s[1], pos$s[2], "+"); text(pos$r[1], pos$r[2], "+")
text(pos$k1[1], pos$k1[2], quote(k[1])); text(pos$k2[1], pos$k2[2], quote(k[2]))
for (n in c("A", "B", "C")) text(pos[[n]][1], pos[[n]][2], bquote(italic(.(n))))
text(pos$fs[1], pos$fs[2], quote(list(f[A], f[B])))
text(pos$fr[1], pos$fr[2], quote(f[C]))
for (n in c("k1", "A", "B")) edge(n, "u")
for (n in c("C", "k2")) edge(n, "v")
edge("u", "s", "-1", side = 2); edge("v", "s")
edge("u", "r"); edge("v", "r", "-1", side = 4)
edge("s", "fs"); edge("r", "fr")
par(op)
```

**Example.** Nodes used twice or more become temporaries:

```cpp
const double _t0 = params[4]*x[2];       // k2*C
const double _t1 = params[3]*x[0]*x[1];  // k1*A*B
const double _t2 = _t0 - _t1;
dxdt[0] = _t2;
dxdt[1] = _t2;
dxdt[2] = -_t0 + _t1;
```

**Derivatives.** Forward and reverse sweeps over the graph form
Jacobian-vector and vector-Jacobian products in time linear in the graph
size [@griewank2008evaluating], as new nodes of the same graph, so
derivative and value share common parts. The reverse contractions
$J^{\mathsf T}\lambda$, $(\partial f/\partial p)^{\mathsf T}\lambda$ are
vector-Jacobian products; Rosenbrock stages and event localization use
Jacobian-vector products along $\dot x = f$.

$J = \partial f/\partial x$ is assembled by entries or by coloring:

- *Entries.* Each state-dependent node holds a sparse state gradient;
  those of the graph roots are the nonzero entries of $J$. The cost
  $W_{\mathrm{ent}} = \sum_{v} |\mathrm{supp}\,\nabla v|$ over the $E_s$
  state-dependent nodes $v$ of $f$ grows with the density of $J$.
- *Coloring*, when $W_{\mathrm{ent}} > \max(4E_s, 50\,000)$. A greedy
  distance-2 coloring of the column intersection graph groups structurally
  orthogonal columns
  [@curtis1974estimation; @coleman1983estimation; @gebremedhin2005color].
  With at most $n_x/4$ colors, one Jacobian-vector product per color,
  seeded with ones on the columns of that color, recovers those columns;
  with more colors, entries are
  kept.

**Linear tables.** A sum of twelve or more terms $c_j\,x_j\,\phi$, numeric
$c_j$, common state-free $\phi$, becomes a row of a constant matrix $C$,
$f(x) = \psi(x, Cx)$. The code evaluates $z = Cx$ once per call from a
sparse or dense table and assembles
[]{#eq-linmap-jacobian}
$$
  J = \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial x} + \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial z}\,C, \tag{1}
$$
while the reverse contractions apply $C^{\mathsf T}$. A dense coupling,
such as a dipolar interaction of all states, costs one table, not a sum
of expressions per entry.

**Loops.** Statements whose graphs agree up to state indices and
constants, such as method-of-lines grid points, form a class. Sixteen or
more instances become one loop over index and constant tables, a sum of
many like terms an inner loop. Differentiation stays per instance, so
generator work grows with the instance count; the emitted code of a
regular model does not.
